section.title: Average rate of change
section.p: A limit of average rates cannot be understood until the average rate itself is clear. We begin with the ordinary slope between two points.
If f is a function and the input changes from a to b, then the output changes from f(a) to f(b). The average rate of change compares these two changes:
Geometrically, this is the slope of the line passing through (a,f(a)) and (b,f(b)), called a secant line.

warning.title: Displacement versus distance
warning.p: Average velocity measures net signed displacement s(b)-s(a) divided by elapsed time, not total distance traveled. A runner starting at 0, running to 100\text{ m}, and returning to 0 in 20\text{ s} has average velocity \frac{0-0}{20} = 0\text{ m/s}.

subsection.title: Average rate from data
subsection.p: A formula is not required; average rates can be computed directly from experimental measurements.

subsection.title: Units of a rate
subsection.p: The units of an average rate always follow the quotient: \frac{\text{output units}}{\text{input units}}.

subsection.p: Average rates describe gross changes across a non-zero interval. To measure what happens at an exact instant, we must shrink the interval to zero—the subject of the next section.
